3: \section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
4: 
5: The main distinction is how a method constructs the uncertainty used to choose
6: an action.  Some methods retain features computed when data arrive; others
7: fix a network linearization, learn a last-layer representation, or update an
8: approximate posterior.  We study a different choice: recomputing every past
9: observation's Jacobian at the current parameter, then relating that current
10: curvature to confidence built from collection-time features.
11: 
12: \paragraph{Confidence from collection-time or fixed features.}
13: Linear UCB \citep{abbasi2011improved} and Thompson sampling
14: \citep{thompson1933likelihood,agrawal2013thompson} provide the statistical basis
15: for many neural-bandit methods.  In their stated algorithms, NeuralUCB
16: \citep{zhou2020neural} and NeuralTS \citep{zhang2021neural} add a gradient
17: feature to the covariance when its observation arrives.  Later network updates
18: do not trigger a replay of all historical gradients in that covariance.
19: 
20: Other methods separate the learned prediction from a fixed reference for
21: uncertainty.  \citet{kassraie2022neural} use initialization-time features for a
22: kernelized NTK reference alongside a trained-network mean.  Their SupNN-UCB
23: variant has a sublinear-regret guarantee under NTK-RKHS,
24: sufficient-exploration, and network-width assumptions.
25: \citet{salgia2023provably} controls adaptivity through grouped histories and a
26: confidence argument relating a finite network to the NTK.
27: \citet{deb2024contextual} instead study online neural regression and
28: contextual-bandit reductions.  These guarantees address their respective
29: feature and data constructions.  Our question is what additional certificates
30: justify using a metric that replays the entire history at each current
31: parameter.
32: 
33: \paragraph{Uncertainty in learned last-layer features.}
34: NeuralLinear maintains Bayesian linear uncertainty in learned final-layer
35: features \citep{riquelme2018deep}.  The methods of \citet{xu2022shallow} and
36: \citet{bui2025variance} use UCB-style linear exploration over learned deep
37: representations.  Their linear uncertainty models concern those representations;
38: recomputing last-layer features is different from constructing a GGN over all
39: network parameters.  Our theorem specifies certificates for the latter
40: transport.  It does not give a general analysis of neural-linear representation
41: learning.
42: 
43: \paragraph{Uncertainty from recursively updated posteriors.}
44: \citet{duranmartin2022efficient} use extended Kalman filter (EKF) updates in a
45: learned or random low-dimensional affine parameter subspace.  A dense or
46: diagonal covariance in that subspace induces a low-rank covariance over
47: parameters spanning all network layers.  Memory does not grow with the number
48: of rounds.  This reduces the space in which uncertainty is represented, rather
49: than applying exact curvature--vector products in the full parameter space.
50: 
51: LO-FI \citep{chang2023lowrank} instead maintains a diagonal-plus-low-rank
52: approximation to the full-parameter posterior precision.  Recursive EKF and
53: online-SVD updates compress the posterior in one pass, without replaying past
54: data; at fixed rank, cost is linear in the parameter count.  The authors use
55: this approximation for Thompson sampling in an MNIST contextual bandit.
56: Our transported-UCB theorem relates current replayed curvature to a separate
57: frozen-feature confidence metric, with explicit factors for approximate
58: operators and solver widths.  Our dense audit evaluates neither compressed
59: operators nor CG and establishes no practical advantage over LO-FI.
60: 
61: \paragraph{Fixed linearizations, Laplace approximations, and sampling.}
62: \citet{maddox2021fast} linearize once around a trained network and use implicit
63: Jacobian/Fisher products with CG for predictive inference.  These implicit
64: solves are closely related to those that could compute our widths, but the
65: reference linearization remains fixed.  A Laplace approximation places a local
66: Gaussian posterior around a MAP solution, using inverse curvature as its
67: covariance \citep{mackay1992practical}.  Last-layer Laplace fixes the backbone
68: and therefore omits uncertainty in its weights \citep{kristiadi2020being}.
69: \citet{daxberger2021laplace} systematize all-weight, subnetwork, and last-layer
70: variants with full, low-rank, Kronecker-factored, or diagonal curvature.
71: Structured all-layer variants use Kronecker-factored curvature
72: \citep{ritter2018scalable,martens2015optimizing}.  These constructions motivate
73: ways to represent predictive uncertainty.  The issue here is sequential
74: validity: whether a current relinearized operator can justify a UCB score when
75: it differs from the predictable confidence Gram.
76: 
77: Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson sampling (LMC-TS) \citep{xu2022langevin} avoids
78: materializing a covariance matrix.  Noisy gradient steps on a regularized loss
79: produce approximate samples from a loss-defined parameter posterior.  Its
80: regret guarantee concerns linear contextual bandits; its neural-bandit evidence
81: is empirical.  The sampling approximation must be controlled at each round.
82: Our theorem has different requirements: certificates for metric transport,
83: operator distortion, and the width used in the score.  The dense audit does
84: not compare computational cost or empirical performance with LMC-TS.
85: 
86: \paragraph{The statistical confidence model.}
87: \citet[Appendix~E]{lattimore2020learning} analyze LinUCB with round-dependent
88: feature sets and an explicit bonus for bounded misspecification.  This is a
89: close connection to the corrected center used here.  Our pseudo-responses
90: in \Cref{eq:pseudo-response-new} turn the nonlinear observations into
91: predictable linear regression with a Taylor remainder and misspecification
92: error.  Adding the current affine offset gives the corrected prediction center.
93: Its confidence argument combines standard self-normalized regression bounds
94: with deterministic bias bounds.  We do not claim a new generic method for
95: misspecified linear confidence.  The further question is how that reference
96: confidence can support current replayed curvature and the numerical width
97: actually used for selection.
98: 
99: \paragraph{The geometric and operator comparisons.}
100: The metric geometry is established.  \citet{thompson1963certain} introduced
101: the part metric now called the Thompson metric on ordered cones, and
102: \citet{nussbaum1994finsler} developed its Finsler structure and applications.
103: On the positive-definite cone, the tangent norm is
104: $\|V^{-1/2}\dot V V^{-1/2}\|_{\rm op}$.  We use the resulting comparison
105: between a path and its endpoints to connect frozen bandit confidence, current
106: replayed GGN/Fisher curvature, approximate operators, and certified solver
107: widths.  The geometry and the path-to-endpoint comparison themselves are not
108: contributions of this paper.
109: 
110: Spectral approximations also have an established role in bandit regret bounds.
111: \citet{kuzborskij2019efficient} replace a linear-bandit Gram matrix with a
112: Frequent Directions sketch and derive bounds in terms of its spectral
113: approximation quality.  They already note that SOFUL may incur linear regret
114: when the spectrum has heavy tails.  Our two-sided operator comparison in
115: \Cref{thm:transported-ucb} plays a similar role: it relates the applied operator
116: to exact current curvature.  A separate path certificate relates that
117: curvature to the frozen-feature confidence metric, and a solver certificate
118: controls the computed width.  We claim no novelty for converting a spectral
119: sandwich into a regret bound, and we do not evaluate a sketched operator.
120: 
121: \paragraph{Computing widths without storing a matrix.}
122: Pearlmutter's algorithm \citep{pearlmutter1994fast} computes exact
123: Hessian--vector products.  The analogous GGN--vector product has the
124: Jacobian-transpose-times-Jacobian-times-vector structure
125: \citep{schraudolph2002fast}.  Influence functions use inverse-curvature--vector
126: products to attribute predictions to training points
127: \citep{koh2017understanding}.  A CG implementation of our solver interface
128: would use the same implicit-solve primitive.  The theorem permits certified
129: operator and solve approximations, but the experiment uses dense current
130: metrics and direct Cholesky solves.  It makes no matrix-free scalability claim.
131: 
132: \paragraph{Weighted Grams and experimental design.}
133: Weighted least-squares Grams appear in the experimental-design analysis of
134: \citet{lattimore2020learning}.  In our scaled-tanh specialization, feature
135: directions are fixed and relinearization changes their positive weights.
136: Comparing those weights term by term gives elementary positive-semidefinite bounds
137: (\Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights}), which we use as an endpoint certificate.
138: The reward model remains fixed during this comparison; a nonstationary reward
139: model would require a separate statistical analysis.
140: 
141: Bandit exploration also connects to classical D-optimal and A-optimal design
142: through objectives such as maximizing $\log\det(\bVbar_t)$ or minimizing
143: the trace of $\bVbar_t^{-1}$ \citep{valko2013finite}.  Stochastic trace and
144: log-determinant estimators offer related matrix-free tools
145: \citep{ubaru2017fast}.  Here the frozen log-determinant enters the regret
146: analysis.  The audited policy chooses actions by its UCB score and does not
147: implement those estimators.
148: 
149: For current full-parameter GGN/Fisher scores, the conditional theorem requires
150: transport from collection-time confidence, bounds on operator distortion, and
151: control of solver error.  Whether this choice is computationally preferable to
152: fixed NTK features, grouped histories, regression reductions, learned last-layer
153: representations, or approximate posterior methods is not established here.
